## 1. The Conceptual Shift: Metric Rectifiability vs. Differential Heuristics

Elementary calculus calculates arc length via $ds = \sqrt{1 + (y')^2} dx$. In metric geometry, curves are rectifiable if and only if their polygonal variations have a finite supremum:
$$\Lambda(\gamma) = \sup_{P} \sum_{i=1}^n d(\gamma(t_i), \gamma(t_{i-1})) < \infty$$
In Riemannian geometry, length is the integral of the pullback metric $L(\gamma) = \int \sqrt{\gamma^* g} dt$.

---

## 2. Numerical Computation: Polygonal Arc Length Integrator

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Python 3
```python
import numpy as np

def polygonal_arc_length(gamma, t0: float, t1: float, n: int) -> float:
    t = np.linspace(t0, t1, n + 1)
    pts = np.array([gamma(ti) for ti in t])
    return float(np.sum(np.linalg.norm(np.diff(pts, axis=0), axis=1)))

# Helix: gamma(t) = (cos t, sin t, t), true length over [0, 2*pi] is 2*pi*sqrt(2)
gamma_helix = lambda t: np.array([np.cos(t), np.sin(t), t])
L = polygonal_arc_length(gamma_helix, 0.0, 2.0 * np.pi, 1000)
print(f"Python 3: Length = {L:.6f} (True: {2.0 * np.pi * np.sqrt(2.0):.6f})")
```

## C++20
```cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
#include <cmath>
#include <iomanip>

int main() {
    int n = 1000;
    double t0 = 0.0, t1 = 2.0 * M_PI;
    double dt = (t1 - t0) / n;
    double length = 0.0;

    auto x = [](double t){ return std::cos(t); };
    auto y = [](double t){ return std::sin(t); };
    auto z = [](double t){ return t; };

    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) {
        double ta = t0 + i * dt, tb = ta + dt;
        double dx = x(tb) - x(ta);
        double dy = y(tb) - y(ta);
        double dz = z(tb) - z(ta);
        length += std::sqrt(dx*dx + dy*dy + dz*dz);
    }
    std::cout << std::fixed << std::setprecision(6);
    std::cout << "C++20:    Length = " << length << "\n";
    return 0;
}
```

## Julia
```julia
n = 1000
t = range(0.0, 2pi, length=n+1)
x = cos.(t); y = sin.(t); z = collect(t)
dx = diff(x); dy = diff(y); dz = diff(z)
L = sum(sqrt.(dx.^2 .+ dy.^2 .+ dz.^2))
println("Julia:    Length = $(round(L, digits=6))")
```

## Modern Fortran
```fortran
program arc_length
  implicit none
  integer, parameter :: n = 1000
  integer :: i
  real(8) :: t0, t1, dt, ta, tb, dx, dy, dz, length, pi

  pi = 3.141592653589793d0
  t0 = 0.0d0; t1 = 2.0d0 * pi
  dt = (t1 - t0) / n
  length = 0.0d0

  do i = 0, n-1
    ta = t0 + i * dt
    tb = ta + dt
    dx = cos(tb) - cos(ta)
    dy = sin(tb) - sin(ta)
    dz = tb - ta
    length = length + sqrt(dx*dx + dy*dy + dz*dz)
  end do

  print '(A,F10.6)', "Fortran:  Length = ", length
end program arc_length
```

## Lean 4
```lean
-- Lean 4: Curves of Bounded Variation and Arc Length in Metric Spaces
import Mathlib.Topology.MetricSpace.Basic

-- Path variation over a finite partition in a metric space
def PathVariation {X : Type*} [PseudoMetricSpace X] (γ : ℝ → X) (pts : List ℝ) : ℝ :=
  match pts with
  | [] => 0
  | [_] => 0
  | a :: b :: rest => dist (γ a) (γ b) + PathVariation γ (b :: rest)

-- A curve is rectifiable if its polygonal variations are bounded above
def IsRectifiable {X : Type*} [PseudoMetricSpace X] (γ : ℝ → X) (a b : ℝ) : Prop :=
  BddAbove { v : ℝ | ∃ pts : List ℝ, pts.Head? = some a ∧ pts.getLast? = some b ∧ v = PathVariation γ pts }
```
